soil-form-076.title: Reading ancient air from ancient soils
soil-form-076.text: Soils form in near-constant contact with the atmosphere, so old soils hold clues to old air. Paleoatmosphere reconstruction uses paleosol chemistry to infer that past composition. How oxidized a paleosol is has served as an indicator of atmospheric oxygen, which has risen over Earth's history. Carbon dioxide has been reconstructed three ways. Researchers use gas exchange between soil and air, carbon isotopes in carbonate nodules formed in the soil, and mass balances of several gases. Researchers on the early Earth are still actively developing these methods.

soil-form-075.title: Ancient soils as rain gauges and thermometers
soil-form-075.text: Rates and styles of weathering depend on climate, so a paleosol can gauge the climate it formed in. Mean annual precipitation and mean annual air temperature are the variables most often reconstructed. Many proxies, measurable stand-ins for a past condition, track chemical changes through the profile during weathering, burial and later alteration. Not every proxy suits every paleosol. Most work only for Phanerozoic paleosols, because landscape processes changed sharply after land plants arose. Proxies for seasonality rely on carbonate formed in the soil as it wets and dries, and they are still being tested and refined.

soil-form-074.title: Naming ancient soils with a modern rulebook
soil-form-074.text: A forest soil could not exist before there were trees. That simple fact shows why paleosol classification is hard. It mostly borrows the top-level orders of the US system, {{ref:soil-class-006}}, because modern systems fit ancient soils poorly. Geology, life and the atmosphere changed greatly over the paleosol record, notably at the Great Oxidation Event 2.42 billion years ago. The forest soil order, {{ref:soil-class-090}}, is also defined by chemical properties that rock does not preserve. That hierarchy cannot be applied to paleosols below the order level. A naming scheme made for paleosols has been proposed but is used only sporadically.

soil-form-073.title: How to recognize a soil turned to stone
soil-form-073.text: How can anyone tell that a layer of rock was once a soil? Paleosol identification answers with criteria. Rye and Holland set out five in 1998. They apply to paleosols of any age. They include formation in place on bedrock, soft-sediment deformation at the top of the profile, and up-profile changes in chemistry, texture and mineralogy that match weathering on land. In the field, signs include horizons, bedrock corestones within finer overlying material, and traces of surface processes such as roots and burrows. Diagnostic horizons and features separate paleosol types. All have an A horizon, but those of the order described in {{ref:soil-class-098}} also have an O horizon above it.

soil-form-069.title: Laterite aquifers: groundwater held in red earth
soil-form-069.text: In rural tropical areas, the bedrock is often impermeable granite, gneiss, schist or sandstone. Water cannot pass through it, so the laterite above becomes the usable store of groundwater. Thick, porous and slightly permeable, these laterite layers hold water and yield it to wells. Sri Lanka's Southwestern Laterite, or Cabook, Aquifer recharges rapidly with the April–May rains and the monsoon, and supports shallow dug wells. In some dense suburbs, its water level can fall to 15 m below ground after more than 65 dry days.

soil-form-068.title: Laterite blocks that harden in the open air
soil-form-068.text: Laterite is mined below the groundwater level while wet and soft, and cut into blocks. As the moisture evaporates, its iron compounds lock into a rigid lattice that resists the weather. Khmer builders used it with sandstone in the Angkor monuments, including the foundations and inner parts of Angkor Wat behind its sandstone face. After 1000 AD, Angkorian construction shifted to rectangular temple enclosures of laterite, brick and stone. Since the mid-1970s, laterite has replaced stone as a road base course in trials. In 1984 Malawi saved US$40,000 per km this way.

soil-form-070.title: Red earth that scrubs phosphorus from wastewater
soil-form-070.text: In Northern Ireland, phosphorus from farms enriches the lakes, and local laterite offers a fix. Rich in iron and aluminum, laterite can remove phosphorus and heavy metals from wastewater. At sewage works, this low-grade aluminum ore is used in acid solution, followed by precipitation. Laboratory tests removed 99% of phosphorus from solution, and a pilot-scale facility removed 96%. Columns of laterite with water percolating through them lowered cadmium, chromium and lead to undetectable concentrations.

soil-form-067.title: Farming laterite soils: rich in clay, poor in nutrients
soil-form-067.text: Laterite soils are rich in clay but heavily leached, an awkward mix for farmers. Their clay helps them hold water and nutrients, and makes them more plastic than sandy soils. It also slows the passage of water, so rain enters slowly. Intensive leaching leaves them less fertile than other soils. Yet they respond readily to manure and irrigation, and suit plantation crops such as oil palm, tea, coffee and cashew. If their structure degrades, a hard surface crust forms. It blocks water entry and seedling emergence and increases runoff. In Niger, 'bio-reclamation of degraded lands', using planting pits, residues and drought-tolerant crops, has rehabilitated degraded laterite soils.

soil-form-071.title: Lateritic ores: metals concentrated by tropical weathering
soil-form-071.text: About 70% of Earth's land-based nickel resources lie in laterites, which currently supply about 40% of world nickel production. Laterites concentrate many metals: aluminum, iron, manganese, nickel, copper and gold. Aluminum is found in the ore described in {{ref:soil-chem-108}}, iron and manganese in iron-rich hard crusts, nickel and copper in disintegrated rock, and gold in mottled clays. That main aluminum ore is a variety of laterite. It averages 45 to 60% Al2O3 and 20 to 30% Fe2O3 by weight. Northern Ireland's basaltic laterites, up to 30 m thick, were once a major source of iron and aluminum ore.

soil-form-086.title: How fast bedrock turns to soil under a growing blanket
soil-form-086.text: The thicker the soil, the more slowly the rock beneath it weathers. The soil production function expresses the rate at which bedrock weathers into soil as a function of soil thickness. A general model has weathering decline exponentially with thickness h: de/dt = P0 exp(−kh). P0 is the maximum weathering rate and k an empirical constant. Temperature swings and average water penetration both fall off exponentially below the surface. At northern California sites P0 ranged from 0.08 to 2.0 mm/yr, and in southeastern Australia from 0.05 to 0.14 mm/yr. Yet k varied little, from 2 to 4 m−1. G.K. Gilbert's older humped model, from 1877, puts the fastest weathering under an intermediate thickness, since bare rock sheds the water that chemical weathering needs.

soil-form-060.title: Lessivage: how clay travels down through a soil
soil-form-060.text: Rain soaking into a soil can carry clay with it. Lessivage, also called argilluviation, is the washing of fine clay from the upper to the lower part of a soil by water moving down through the soil. It is the main mechanism forming the clay-enriched argic, or Bt, horizon of Luvisolic soils. Clay particles carry a negative charge. Infiltrating water picks them up as a colloidal suspension and carries them down until a change in conditions makes them clump together and settle. Clay settles where water stagnates or meets positive ions deeper down. As it accumulates, pores in the illuvial horizon become finer and trap still more clay. Texture matters. Lessivage is most common in medium-textured soils under moderate to high rainfall, especially beneath deciduous and mixed forests, whose organic acids disperse clay. Very sandy soils drain too fast and lack clay. Clay-rich soils drain so slowly that clay moves only a short way. The process is widespread in central and eastern Canada, parts of Europe and temperate Asia. Its results cut both ways. The deposited clay helps the subsoil hold nutrients, but a thick clay-rich layer can make soils prone to compaction, surface ponding and restricted root growth. If the layer becomes too compacted, limiting traffic, deep loosening and tile drainage may be needed.

soil-form-081.title: Ferrallitisation: why so many tropical soils are red
soil-form-081.text: Many tropical soils are red, and ferrallitisation explains why. It is the process that turns rock into a soil of {{ref:soil-chem-088}} clay and sesquioxides, the hydrated oxides of iron and aluminum. In the humid tropics, with consistently high temperatures and rainfall, chemical weathering breaks rock down rapidly into clays. Those clays later break down further, releasing silica. The silica is leached away, while the iron and aluminum sesquioxides remain and give the soil its characteristic red. The process is the reverse of podsolisation, in which silica remains and iron and aluminum are removed. Climate decides the details. Year-round rain in tropical rainforests produces ferrallitic soils, while savannas with alternating wet and dry seasons have ferruginous soils.

soil-form-052.title: Leaching efficiency: why some salty clays resist reclamation
soil-form-052.text: Dense clay in Portugal's Tagus delta proved so hard to flush of salt that it was left as coarse pasture. Its leaching efficiency measured only 0.10 to 0.15. This parameter of the leaching model departs from one where salt is unevenly distributed or the soil's build is irregular. Clay soil in Egypt's Nile delta does much better, at 0.7 to 0.8. Hard to measure directly, it is calibrated by fitting model curves to observed salt levels, giving a value of about 0.75 at Mashtul. Tabulated values run from 0.80 for Tunisian silty clay down to between 0.11 and 0.20 for some clays in Peru, Portugal and Thailand.

soil-form-084.title: Stone lines: geology or the work of burrowers?
soil-form-084.text: Few Earth-science topics have caused more controversy than the stone line. The argument spans archaeology, geology, geomorphology, ecology and pedology, on every continent but Antarctica. At issue is whether stonelayers formed by geological processes or by soil-forming, largely biological, ones. Sharpe coined 'stone-line' in 1938 from South Carolina, reading it as abiotic mass transfer on slopes. He was unaware of earlier names and drawings, including Darwin's. Others have read it as glacial evidence, or as an eroded pavement buried under tropical loess. Morrás and colleagues argued in 2009 that it is the base of soil biomantles. The literature remains divided, and an interpreter's view often reflects background and training.

soil-form-058.title: Why most prehistoric artifacts lie in a churned layer
soil-form-058.text: Most prehistoric cultural materials lie in the soil biomantle, where animal mixing has moved them out of their original context. The exceptions are a few stratified caves and rare open-air sites buried faster than the mixing could destratify them. Artifacts wider than burrows, such as cleavers, core-stones and grinding stones, settle downward and join the basal stonelayer. Smaller flakes spread through the upper biomantle and turn up in the spoil heaps of gophers, moles and mole-rats. Since Darwin, the earthworm has been recognized as a key mixer of biomantles and the artifacts in them.

soil-form-056.title: Gophers, termites and worms: three ways animals rework soil
soil-form-056.text: A pocket gopher, a termite and a worm all rework soil, but in different ways. Animal mixing in the biomantle has three overlapping sub-processes, which together abrade and break down particles, a process called particle comminution. Biomixing is churning by burrowing vertebrates such as pocket gophers, moles, badgers, wombats, aardvarks and pigs, and tree uprooting matters too. Biotransfer moves soil to the surface or within the biomantle, mainly by 'conveyor-belt' ants, termites and worms. Termites may dig many meters for mound-building soil. In biosorting, burrowers move only particles smaller than their burrows, so larger stones settle into a stonelayer at the biomantle's base. Invertebrates are the main biosorters in tropical soils. Small burrowing vertebrates dominate in many midlatitude deserts, prairies and steppes.

soil-form-057.title: Dynamic denudation: everything happening in the biomantle at once
soil-form-057.text: Plants' role in soil formation is well understood. The role of animals in making soil, horizons, the features in {{ref:soil-water-133}} and stone lines was poorly understood until recently. Dynamic denudation is the sum of all processes acting in the soil biomantle. They include organic matter production, eluviation and illuviation, weathering, erosion and deposition, freeze–thaw, shrinking and swelling, and gravity movements. Normally all are subsidiary to animal mixing. Wilkinson and Humphreys offer evidence that this mixing appears to be the most active soil-forming process in many soils. It dominates the upper part of most soils, except possibly the soils of {{ref:soil-class-106}} and {{ref:soil-class-024}}.

soil-form-062.title: Cheluviation: metals ride organic carriers downward
soil-form-062.text: A gray-white leached layer above a dark brown or red one is a typical signature of cheluviation. In this process, metal ions in the upper soil bind with organic molecules called ligands, forming chelates. The chelates move downward by eluviation and are then deposited. Iron, aluminum, manganese, calcium, magnesium and trace elements can all be chelated, mostly by ligands from soil organic matter. Chelates with the organic acid described in {{ref:soil-chem-060}} leach and deposit strongly. Iron and aluminum move easily at low pH and under reducing conditions, but precipitate as pH rises to around 7–8 or under oxidizing conditions. Clay adsorbs chelates and weakens their leaching, while coarse-textured or water-saturated soils enhance it.

soil-form-078.title: Soil memory: a record written over and over
soil-form-078.text: Dokuchaev called soil 'a mirror of the landscape'. In 1953 Nikiforoff echoed him with a new term, soil memory: the idea that soil keeps a record of past natural changes, environmental conditions and human activity. Soils store that record like a page written over and over, with newer features overprinting older ones. This is pedomemory; layered sediments instead store lithomemory, like a book in datable order. The idea is used to study climate change, land-use history and archaeological evidence. Persistent environmental DNA in cultivated soils is read as a 'memory effect'. Yet most soils have developed under more than one set of conditions, so the record is partial and 'censored'. Equifinality, different paths leading to the same result, complicates reading it, and the concept serves as an exploratory tool.

soil-form-079.title: Bacteria that remember an Iron Age village
soil-form-079.text: Distinctive bacterial communities still mark an Iron Age settlement in Sicily, Iron Age cremation burials, medieval activity areas and Neolithic ditch infills. Microbial soil memory is the ability of soil microbes to change their community structure, diversity and activity, and to keep those changes over time. Many bacteria survive in dormant states for long periods, persisting through large environmental changes. PCR and next-generation sequencing characterize soil bacterial communities from their DNA, and they are well suited to detecting traces of past influences.

soil-form-077.title: Polygenetic soils: one profile, several histories
soil-form-077.text: Most soils carry more than one history. A polygenetic soil, such as a paleosol, shows evidence of continued soil development under later conditions. Most soils are polygenetic, so a younger soil-forming signal may overprint, mask or erase an older one. Examples with ancient clay-enriched horizons include the Wounded Moose paleosol of the Yukon and the Berino Paleosol of New Mexico. The soil described in {{ref:soil-class-051}} has been proposed to be polygenetic. Its altered parent material includes volcanic ash, non-carbonate sediments and wind-blown sediments.

reviews.how-soils-form: Soil formation begins with weathering of parent material and answers to five intertwined factors: climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time. Dokuchaev and then Jenny wrote those factors as equations, and slopes arrange their effects into catenas while chronosequences isolate time. Water moving down the profile does much of the building, by leaching dissolved material, washing clay down in lessivage, and stripping sesquioxides in podzolisation or leaving them behind in red laterites. Burrowing life pushes the other way, churning the biomantle, sinking stones into stonelayers and blurring the horizons that water builds. Soils formed long ago survive as paleosols, polygenetic records of past climates and atmospheres that later development can overprint.
